what_it_survives: losing this hosting provider. The in-database copy survives a container replacement, a redeploy and a crash; it does not survive the provider, which is the failure #51 names
why_a_round_trip: a backup nobody has restored is a hope. The gate reads export, upload, read back, decrypt and restore into a scratch database -- not a URL being set. A typed bucket address that is wrong, or whose credentials are, survives losing the provider exactly as well as no bucket at all
encryption: AES-256-CBC with a stretched passphrase, sealed by `archive` itself before upload and authenticated before decryption, with the key in a variable the bucket credentials do not include. A reader who obtains the bucket gets ciphertext
retention: prune deletes beyond 14 from this system's own record, which needs delete permission on the bucket key. A key without it (safer) leaves old archives in place; a bucket lifecycle rule should then own retention. B2 keeps every version by default, so even a permitted delete only hides a file until a lifecycle rule removes it
provider_neutral: written against the S3 API, so Backblaze B2, Cloudflare R2, Wasabi and AWS are a URL rather than a code change. A continuity plan welded to one vendor has moved the single point of failure rather than removed it
